newsitem.title: JAPAN: Sony move may cloud outlook for digital video disc.
newsitem.headline: Sony move may cloud outlook for digital video disc.

text.p: A fresh dispute among developers of digital video discs (DVD) could undermine the hot new technology's fledgling market, analysts said on Wednesday.

A global 10-firm agreement on a standard format for DVD-RAM (random-access memory) discs fell apart when Sony Corp and two other companies announced on Wednesday morning that they would support a separate format.

Sales of DVD products, designed to replace much bulkier video tapes, CDs and CD-ROMs, have been sluggish since debuting on the global market early this year, because the discs' read-only memory (ROM) does not allow users to record music, video or other data, and few pre-recorded titles are currently available.

Industry officials expected DVD-RAM drives, due to hit the market late this year, to help solve this problem and boost DVD sales. The drives should let users record or rewrite data from CD-ROMs, while the recording of audio-visual content may also be possible eventually.
Analysts said, however, that the move by Sony, Philips Electronics NVand Hewlett-Packard Co to a new format could deal a setback to DVD-RAM, at least in the short term.

"(As) the disintegration of the agreement will certainly confuse consumers, the news is likely to have a short-term negative impact on acceptance of DVD-RAM products," BZW Japan analyst Hiroshi Takada said.
Masahiro Ono, analyst at Credit Lyonnais Securities, played down such worries, however, saying he expected DVD-RAM would take a long time to evolve into a major market.
"At the moment, personal computers equipped with DVD-RAMs are unlikely to become common for another four to five years," he said. "The companies are not really pressed to standardise specifications."
A Sony spokesman said on Wednesday that Sony, Philips and Hewlett-Packard applied in May to the European Computer Manufacturers Association for approval of their new DVD-RAM specifications.
He said he did not know when the association would give its approval, although it would probably take six months to a year.

Sony's announcement shocked other DVD developers, which include Matsushita Electric Industrial Co Ltd , Mitsubishi Electric Corp , Victor Co of Japan , Toshiba Corp , Pioneer Electronic Corp , Hitachi Ltd , Thomson SA and Time Warner Inc .
"We are surprised. But as we do not know the details yet, we cannot comment further," a Matsushita spokesman said.
The Sony spokesman said his firm would remain a member of the group but does not plan to introduce products based on the common format.

He said the Sony group's DVD-RAM format is more compatible than the common format with DVD-ROMs currently in use and offers a data storage capacity of 3.0 gigabits, compared with the common format's 2.6 gigabits.
Even before Wednesday's news, the 10 DVD developers had already been at odds over how to divide royalties and licensing fees for DVD technology.

In April, Sony said it joined with Philips and Pioneer to begin licensing their manufacturing technology for DVDs for a royalty of 3.5 percent for DVD players and five U.S. cents per disc. The decision was made without the approval of other members of the consortium.

Obtaining a licence from the three companies would not be sufficient to allow a company to begin making DVD products because patents held by them cover only part of the technology needed to make the products.
